Item 1.    Business

Overview

    Blackstone is the world’s largest alternave asset manager. We seek to deliver compelling returns for instuonal and individual
investors by strengthening the companies and assets in which we invest. Our more than $1.3 trillion in Total Assets Under Management
as of December 31, 2025 include global investment strategies focused on real estate, private equity, infrastructure, life sciences, growth
equity, credit, real assets, secondaries and hedge funds.

     Our businesses use a soluons-oriented approach to drive beer performance. We believe our scale, diversiﬁed business, long record
of investment performance, rigorous investment process and strong client relaonships posion us to connue to perform well in a
variety of market condions, expand our assets under management, and innovate.

     We invest across asset classes on behalf of our investors, including pension funds, insurance companies and individual investors. Our
mission is to fulﬁll our ﬁduciary duty by creang long-term value for our investors. We aim to do this by strengthening the companies,
real estate assets and other investments in our porolio, equipping them to thrive in the global economy. To the extent our funds
perform well, we can support a beer rerement for tens of millions of pensioners, including teachers, nurses and ﬁreﬁghters.

    As of December 31, 2025, we employed approximately 5,285 people, including our 268 senior managing directors, at our
headquarters in New York and around the world. Our employees are integral to Blackstone’s culture of integrity, professionalism and
excellence. We believe hiring, training and retaining talented individuals, coupled with our rigorous investment process, has supported
our excellent investment record over many years. This record, in turn, has enabled us to innovate into new strategies, drive growth and
beer serve our investors.

Business Segments

    Our four business segments are: (a) Real Estate, (b) Private Equity, (c) Credit & Insurance and (d) Mul-Asset Invesng. Informaon
about our business segments should be read together with “Part II. Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condion
and Results of Operaons.” For more informaon concerning the revenues and fees we derive from our business segments, see “—Fee
Structure/Incenve Arrangements.”

Real Estate

    Our Real Estate business is a global leader in real estate invesng, with $319.3 billion of Total Assets Under Management as of
December 31, 2025. Our Real Estate business operates as one globally integrated business with approximately 785 employees and has
investments across the globe, including in the Americas, Europe and Asia. Our real estate investment teams seek to ulize our global
experse and presence to generate aracve risk-adjusted returns for our investors.

    Our Blackstone Real Estate Partners (“BREP”) business is geographically diversiﬁed and targets a broad range of opportunisc real
estate and real estate-related investments. The BREP plaorm includes global funds as well as funds focused speciﬁcally on Europe or
Asia investments. BREP seeks to invest themacally in high-quality, well-located assets where we see outsized growth potenal driven by
global economic and demographic trends. BREP has made signiﬁcant investments in logiscs, data centers, rental housing, hospitality,
oﬃce and retail properes around the world, as well as in a variety of real estate operang companies.

                                                                                                                                             7
    Our Core+ real estate strategy invests in substanally stabilized real estate globally, primarily through perpetual capital vehicles. The
strategy includes our (a) Blackstone Property Partners (“BPP”) funds, which are focused on high-quality assets in the Americas, Europe
and Asia and (b) a non-listed real estate investment trust (“REIT”), Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust, Inc. (“BREIT”), and Blackstone
European Property Income Fund (“BEPIF”) vehicles, which provide income-focused individual investors access to instuonal quality real
estate primarily in the Americas and Europe, respecvely.

     Our Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies (“BREDS”) plaorm primarily targets real estate-related debt investment opportunies.
BREDS invests in both public and private markets, primarily in the U.S. and Europe. BREDS’ scale and investment mandates enable it to

Private Equity

     Our Private Equity segment encompasses global businesses with a total of approximately 720 employees managing $416.4 billion of
Total Assets Under Management as of December 31, 2025. Our Private Equity segment includes: (a) Private Equity Strategies (described
below), (b) Infrastructure, which includes (1) our infrastructure-focused funds for instuonal investors with a primary focus on the U.S.
and Europe (Blackstone Infrastructure Partners or “BIP”) and (2) a private wealth-focused plaorm oﬀering eligible individual investors
access to our infrastructure capabilies (Blackstone Infrastructure Strategies or “BXINFRA”), (c) our secondaries business (“Secondaries”),
which includes Strategic Partners Fund Soluons (“Strategic Partners”) and our GP Stakes business (“Blackstone GP Stakes” or “BXGP”),
(d) our capital markets services business (Blackstone Capital Markets or “BXCM”) and (e) a private wealth-focused plaorm oﬀering
eligible individuals exposure to certain of Blackstone’s key illiquid investment strategies through a single commitment (Blackstone Total
Alternaves Soluon or “BTAS”).

    Our Private Equity Strategies include: (a) our Corporate Private Equity business (described below), (b) our hybrid capital investment
plaorm that invests ﬂexibly across asset classes, industries and geographies (Blackstone Taccal Opportunies or “Taccal
Opportunies”), (c) our life sciences investment plaorm (Blackstone Life Sciences or “BXLS”), (d) our growth equity investment plaorm
(Blackstone Growth or “BXG”) and (e) a private wealth-focused plaorm oﬀering eligible individual investors access to Blackstone’s
private equity capabilies (Blackstone Private Equity Strategies Fund or “BXPE”).

    Our Corporate Private Equity business consists of: (a) our global private equity funds (Blackstone Capital Partners or “BCP”), (b) our
Asia-focused private equity funds (Blackstone Capital Partners Asia or “BCP Asia”), (c) our sector-focused funds, including our energy- and
energy transion-focused funds (Blackstone Energy Transion Partners or “BETP”) and (d) our core private equity funds (Blackstone Core
Equity Partners or “BCEP”).

    We are a global leader in private equity invesng. Our Corporate Private Equity business pursues transacons across industries on a
global basis. It strives to create value by invesng in great businesses where our capital, strategic insight, global relaonships and
operaonal support can drive transformaon. Corporate Private Equity’s investment strategies and core themes connually evolve in
ancipaon of, or in response to, changes in the global economy, local markets, regulaon, capital ﬂows and geopolical trends. We seek
to construct a diﬀerenated porolio of investments with a well-deﬁned, post-acquision value creaon strategy. Similarly, we seek
investments that can generate strong unlevered returns regardless of entry or exit cycle ming. BCEP pursues control-oriented
investments in high-quality companies with durable businesses and seeks to oﬀer a lower level of risk and a longer hold period than
tradional private equity.

    Taccal Opportunies pursues a themacally driven, hybrid capital investment strategy. Our ﬂexible, global mandate enables us to

      BXLS invests across the life cycle of companies and products within the life sciences sector. BXLS primarily focuses on investments in

Investment Process and Risk Management

    We maintain a rigorous investment process across all our investment vehicles. Each investment vehicle has investment policies and
procedures that generally contain requirements, guidelines and limitaons for investments, such as limitaons relang to the amount
that will be invested in any one investment and the types of assets, industries or geographic regions in which the vehicle will invest, as
well as limitaons required by law.

    Our investment professionals are responsible for idenfying, evaluang, underwring, diligencing, negoang, execung, managing
and exing investments. For those of our businesses with review commiees and/or investment commiees, such commiees review
and evaluate investment opportunies in a framework that includes a qualitave and quantave assessment of the key risks of
investments. In such businesses, investment professionals generally submit investment opportunies for review and approval by a review
commiee and/or investment commiee, subject to delineated excepons set forth in applicable investment commiee charters or
resoluons. Review and investment commiees are generally comprised of senior leaders and other senior professionals of the
applicable investment business, and in many cases, other senior leaders of Blackstone and its businesses. Consideraons that review and
investment commiees take into account when evaluang an investment may include, without limitaon and depending on the nature of
the invesng business and its strategy, the quality of the business or asset in which the fund proposes to invest, the quality of the
management team, likely exit strategies and factors that could reduce the value of the business or asset at exit, the ability of the business
in which the investment is made to service debt in a range of economic and interest rate environments, macroeconomic trends in the
relevant geographic region or industry and the quality of the businesses’ operaons. In addion, certain of our business units maintain
their own sustainability policies that address, among other things, sustainability factors applicable to their respecve investment
strategies. Exisng investments are reviewed and monitored on a regular basis by investment and asset management professionals. In
addion, our investment professionals and Porolio Operaons professionals work with our porolio company senior execuves to
idenfy opportunies to drive operaonal eﬃciencies and growth.

     Before our BXMA and Secondaries teams decide to invest in an investment fund or an alternave asset manager, as applicable, they
conduct diligence in a number of areas. Depending on the nature of the investment, these areas may include, among others, the
fund’s/manager’s performance, investment terms, investment strategy and investment personnel, as well as its operaons, processes,
risk management and internal controls. With respect to liquid credit clients and other clients whose porolios are acvely traded in our
Credit & Insurance segment, our industry-focused research analysts provide the review and/or investment commiee with a formal and
comprehensive review of new investment recommendaons and porolio managers and trading professionals discuss, among other
things, risks associated with overall porolio composion. Our Credit & Insurance segment’s research team monitors the operang
performance of underlying issuers, while porolio managers, together with our traders, focus on opmizing asset composion to
maximize value for our investors. This investment process is assisted by a variety of proprietary and non-proprietary research models and
methods.

Fee Structure/Incenve Arrangements

Management Fees

   The following is a general descripon of the management fees earned by Blackstone. Management fees are generally based on an
annual rate but payable on a regular basis (typically monthly or quarterly). Management fees received are not subject to clawback.

   •       In our carry funds, the investment adviser or AIFM (depending on the domicile of the fund) receives a management fee based
           on a percentage of the fund’s capital commitments, invested capital and/or undeployed capital during the investment period
           and the fund’s invested capital, investment fair value or capital commitments a er the investment period. Management fees
           are generally payable over either the term or life of the fund. Depending on the fee basis, negave performance of one or
           more investments in the fund may reduce the total management fee paid for the relevant period, but not the fee rate.
   •       In our other fund structures, unless outlined diﬀerently below, the investment adviser or AIFM (depending on the domicile of
           the fund) receives a management fee based on a percentage of the fund’s net asset value over the term or life of the fund.
           These funds may permit investors to withdraw or redeem their interests periodically, in some cases following the expiraon of
           a speciﬁed period of me when capital may not be withdrawn. Decreases in net asset value reduce the total management fee
           paid for the relevant period, but not the fee rate.
   •       In our CLOs, the investment adviser typically receives a base management fee and a subordinated management fee, which are
           calculated as a percentage of the CLO’s assets. Although varying from deal to deal, a CLO will typically be wound down within
           eight to eleven years of being launched. The amount of fees will decrease as the CLO deleverages toward the end of its term.
   •       In our separately managed accounts, the investment adviser generally receives a management fee based on a percentage of
           each account’s net asset value or invested capital. Such management fees are generally subject to contractual rights the
           investor has to terminate our management on generally as short as 30 days’ noce.
   •       In our credit-focused registered investment companies and our BDCs, the investment adviser typically receives a management
           fee based on a percentage of net asset value or total managed assets. Such management fees are generally subject to
           contractual rights of the company’s board of directors to terminate our management of an account on as short as 30 days’
           noce.
   •       For BXMT, the investment adviser receives a management fee based on a percentage of BXMT’s net proceeds received from
           equity oﬀerings and accumulated “distributable earnings” (which is generally equal to its net income, calculated under GAAP,
           excluding certain non-cash and other items), subject to certain adjustments.

    For addional informaon regarding the management fee rates we receive, see “Part II. Item 7. Management’s Discussion and
Analysis of Financial Condion and Results of Operaons — Crical Accounng Policies — Revenue Recognion — Management and
Advisory Fees, Net.”

Incenve Arrangements

    Our incenve arrangements are composed of (a) contractual incenve fees received from certain investment vehicles upon achieving
speciﬁed cumulave investment returns (“Incenve Fees”), and (b) a disproporonate allocaon of the income generated by investment
vehicles otherwise allocable to investors upon achieving certain investment returns (“Performance Allocaons,” and, together with
Incenve Fees, “Performance Revenues”).

    In our carry funds, our Performance Revenues consist of the Performance Allocaons to which the general partner or an aﬃliate
thereof is entled, commonly referred to as carried interest. Our ability to generate and realize carried interest is an important element
of our business and has historically accounted for a very signiﬁcant poron of our income.

    Carried interest is typically structured as a net proﬁts interest in the applicable fund. In the case of our carry funds, carried interest is
generally calculated on a “realized gain” basis, and each general partner (or aﬃliate) is generally entled to an allocaon of up to 20% of
the net realized income and gains (generally taking into account realized and unrealized or net unrealized losses) generated by such fund.
Net realized income or loss is not generally need between or among funds, and in some cases our carry funds provide for allocaons to
be made on current income distribuons (subject to certain condions).

    For most carry funds, the carried interest is subject to a preferred limited partner return generally ranging from 5% to 8% per year,
subject to a catch-up allocaon to the general partner. Some of our carry funds do not provide for a preferred return, and generally the
terms of our carry funds vary in certain respects across our business units and vintages. If, at the end of the life of a carry fund (or earlier
with respect to certain of our carry funds), as a result of diminished performance of later investments in a carry fund’s life, (a) the general
partner receives in excess of the relevant carried interest percentage(s) applicable to the fund as applied to the fund’s cumulave net
proﬁts over the life of the fund, or (in certain cases) (b) the carry fund has not achieved investment returns that exceed the preferred
return threshold (if applicable), then we will be obligated to repay an amount equal to the carried interest that was previously distributed
to us that exceeds the amounts to which we were ulmately entled, up to the amount of carried interest received on an a er-tax basis.
This is known as a “clawback” obligaon and is an obligaon of any person who received such carried interest, including us and other
parcipants in our carried interest plans.

     Although a poron of any dividends paid to our stockholder may include any carried interest received by us, we do not intend to seek
fulﬁllment of any clawback obligaon by seeking to have our stockholders return any poron of such dividends aributable to carried
interest associated with any clawback obligaon. To the extent we are required to fulﬁll a clawback obligaon, however, we may
determine to decrease the amount of our dividends to our stockholders. The clawback obligaon operates with respect to a given carry
fund’s own net investment performance only and carried interest of other funds is not need for determining this conngent obligaon.
Moreover, although a clawback obligaon is several, the governing agreements of most of our funds provide that to the extent another
recipient of carried interest (such as a current or former employee) does not fund his or her respecve share of the clawback obligaon
then due, then we and our employees who parcipate in such carried interest plans may have to fund addional amounts (generally an
addional 50% to 70% beyond our pro-rata share of such obligaon) although we retain the right to pursue any remedies that we have
under such governing agreements against those carried interest recipients who fail to fund their obligaons. We have recorded a
conngent repayment obligaon equal to the amount that would be due on December 31, 2025, if the various carry funds were
liquidated at their current carrying value. For addional informaon concerning the clawback obligaons we could face, see “—Item 1A.
Risk Factors — Risks Related to Our Business — We may not have suﬃcient cash to pay back “clawback” obligaons if and when they are
triggered under the governing agreements with our investors.”

Compeon

     The asset management industry is intensely compeve, and we expect it to remain so. We compete both globally and on a regional,
industry and sector basis. We compete on the basis of a number of factors, including investment performance, transacon execuon
skills, access to capital, access to and retenon of qualiﬁed personnel, reputaon, range of products and services, innovaon and price.

    We face compeon in the pursuit of instuonal and individual investors for our investment funds. Although over me many
instuonal and individual investors have increased the amount of capital they commit to alternave investment funds, such increases
may create increased compeon with respect to fees charged by our funds. In the private wealth and insurance channels, the market for
capital is highly compeve, requires signiﬁcant investment and is highly regulated, which could create compeve challenges for us. In
addion, compeon for fundraising in the private wealth and insurance channels is also driven by the willingness of certain of our
competors to charge lower fees or pay higher or diﬀerent types of distributors fees.

    We also face compeon in the pursuit of aracve investment opportunies for our funds. Depending on the investment, we face
compeon primarily from sponsors managing other funds, investment vehicles and other pools of capital, other ﬁnancial instuons
and instuonal investors (including sovereign wealth and pension funds), corporate buyers and other pares. Several of these
competors have signiﬁcant amounts of capital and many of them have investment objecves similar to ours, which may create
addional compeon for investment opportunies. Some of these competors may also have a lower cost of capital and access to
funding sources or other resources that are not available to us, which may create compeve disadvantages for us with respect to
investment opportunies. In addion, some of these competors may have higher risk tolerances, diﬀerent risk assessments or lower
return thresholds, which could allow them to consider a wider variety of investments and to bid more aggressively than us for
investments. Corporate buyers may be able to achieve synergisc cost savings with regard to an investment or be perceived by sellers as

Item 1A. Risk Factors

Risks Related to Our Business

Diﬃcult market, economic and geopolical condions can adversely aﬀect our business in many ways, each of which could materially
reduce our revenue, earnings and cash ﬂow and adversely aﬀect our ﬁnancial prospects and condion.

    Our business is materially aﬀected by ﬁnancial market and economic condions and events throughout the world that are outside
our control. We may not be able to or may choose not to manage our exposure to these condions and/or events. Such condions
and/or events can adversely aﬀect our business in many ways, including reducing the ability of our funds to raise or deploy capital,
reducing the value or performance of our funds’ investments and making it more diﬃcult for our funds to exit and realize value from
exisng investments. This could in turn materially reduce our revenue, earnings and cash ﬂow and adversely aﬀect our ﬁnancial prospects
and condion. In addion, in the face of a diﬃcult market or economic environment, we may need to reduce our ﬁxed costs and other
expenses in order to maintain proﬁtability. This may include cu ng back or eliminang the use of certain services or service providers, or
terminang the employment of a signiﬁcant number of our personnel that, in each case, could be important to our business and without
which our operang results could be adversely aﬀected. A failure to manage or reduce our costs and other expenses within a me frame
suﬃcient to match any decrease in proﬁtability would adversely aﬀect our operang performance.

     Turmoil in the global ﬁnancial markets can provoke signiﬁcant volality of equity and debt securies prices. This can have a material
and rapid impact on our mark-to-market valuaons, parcularly with respect to our public holdings and credit investments. As publicly
traded equity securies have in recent years represented a meaningful proporon of the assets of many of our funds, stock market
volality, including a sharp decline in the stock market, may adversely aﬀect our results, including our revenues and net income.
Moreover, our public equity holdings have at mes been concentrated in a few large posions, thereby making our unrealized
mark-to-market valuaons parcularly sensive to sharp changes in the price of any of these posions. Further, although the equity
markets are not the only means by which we exit investments, periods of challenging equity markets make it more diﬃcult for our funds
to realize value from investments.

    Geopolical concerns and other global events outside of our control have contributed and may connue to contribute to volale
global equity and debt markets. These concerns and events include, without limitaon, trade conﬂict, civil unrest, threats to naonal
security, and naonal and internaonal security events (including war, terrorist acts or other hoslies). Geopolical instability has been
prevalent in recent years, and 2025 was a year of signiﬁcant geopolical events, including, among others, trade tensions resulng from
U.S. tariﬀ implementaon and retaliatory tariﬀs by other countries and ongoing armed conﬂicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.

     Addionally, the economic outlook for 2026 remains uncertain. Gradual decreases in interest rates during 2025, coupled with
resilience in the U.S. economy, contributed to improved investor senment, stronger capital markets and increased transacon acvity
toward the end of 2025. Nevertheless, inﬂaon has remained above the U.S. Federal Reserve’s target level, and interest rates remain
elevated. Uncertainty regarding the further trajectory of inﬂaon and interest rates creates the potenal for volality in debt and equity
markets. Such volality can contribute to economic deceleraon or contracon in the rate of growth in certain industries, sectors or
geographies, and in turn, poor ﬁnancial results for our funds’ porolio companies or assets and lower investment returns for our funds.
The valuaons of our funds’ real estate assets, and fundraising in certain of our real estate strategies targeng high-net-worth investors,
have been adversely impacted in recent years by elevated interest rates and a high, albeit declining, cost of capital. A slower-than-
expected decrease in interest rates would connue to present a challenge to real estate valuaons. Such factors are even more
challenging in the life science oﬃce and tradional oﬃce market, as well as other properes with long-term leases that do not provide for
short-term rent increases. This has adversely impacted, and may further adversely impact, the performance of certain of our real estate
funds.

performance of other funds are not need for determining this conngent obligaon.

    Adverse economic condions may increase the likelihood that one or more of our carry funds may be subject to clawback obligaons.

Risk management acvies may adversely aﬀect the return on our funds’ investments.

    When managing our exposure to market risks, we may (on our own behalf or on behalf of our funds) from me to me use forward
contracts, opons, swaps, caps, collars and ﬂoors or pursue other strategies or use other forms of derivave instruments to limit our
exposure to changes in the relave values of investments that may result from market developments, including changes in prevailing
interest rates, currency exchange rates and commodity prices. The use of derivave ﬁnancial instruments and other risk management
strategies may not be properly designed to hedge, manage or otherwise reduce the risks we have idenﬁed. In addion, we may not be
able to idenfy, or may not have fully idenﬁed, all applicable material market risks to which we are exposed. We may also choose not to
hedge, in whole or in part, any of the risks that have been idenﬁed. The success of any hedging or other derivaves transacons
generally will depend on our ability to correctly predict market changes, the degree of correlaon between price movements of a
derivave instrument, the posion being hedged, the creditworthiness of the counterparty and other factors, some of which may be
beyond our ability to hedge. As a result, while we may enter into a transacon in order to reduce our exposure to market risks, the
unintended market changes may result in poorer overall investment performance than if it had not been executed. Such transacons may
also limit the opportunity for gain if the value of a hedged posion increases.

     While such hedging arrangements may reduce certain risks, such arrangements themselves may entail certain other risks. These
arrangements may require the posng of cash collateral at a me when a fund has insuﬃcient cash or illiquid assets such that the posng
of the cash is either impossible or requires the sale of assets at prices that do not reﬂect their underlying value. In addion, if our
derivave counterpares or clearinghouses fail to meet their obligaons with respect to the posng of cash collateral, our eﬀorts to
migate certain risks may be ineﬀecve. Moreover, these hedging arrangements may generate signiﬁcant transacon costs, including
potenal tax costs, that reduce the returns generated by a fund.

receivable agreements, including tax beneﬁts aributable to payments under the tax receivable agreements. This payment obligaon is
an obligaon of Blackstone Inc. and/or its wholly owned subsidiaries and not of Blackstone Holdings. As such, the cash distribuons to
public stockholders may vary from holders of Blackstone Holdings Partnership Units (held by Blackstone personnel and others) to the
extent payments are made under the tax receivable agreements to selling holders of Blackstone Holdings Partnership Units. As the
payments reﬂect actual tax savings received by Blackstone enes, there may be a ming diﬀerence between the tax savings received by
Blackstone enes and the cash payments to selling holders of Blackstone Holdings Partnership Units. While the actual increase in tax
basis, as well as the amount and ming of any payments under these agreements, will vary depending upon a number of factors,
including the ming of exchanges, the price of our common stock at the me of the exchange, the extent to which such exchanges are
taxable and the amount and ming of our income, we expect that as a result of the size of the increases in the tax basis of the tangible
and intangible assets of Blackstone Holdings, the payments that we may make under the tax receivable agreements will be substanal.
The payments under a tax receivable agreement are not condioned upon a tax receivable agreement counterparty’s connued
ownership of us. We may need to incur debt to ﬁnance payments under the tax receivable agreements to the extent our cash resources
are insuﬃcient to meet our obligaons under the tax receivable agreements as a result of ming discrepancies or otherwise.

     Although we are not aware of any issue that would cause the IRS to challenge a tax basis increase, the tax receivable agreement
counterpares will not reimburse us for any payments previously made under the tax receivable agreements. As a result, in certain
circumstances payments to the counterpares under the tax receivable agreements could be in excess of our actual cash tax savings. Our
ability to achieve beneﬁts from any tax basis increase, and the payments to be made under the tax receivable agreements, will depend
upon a number of factors, as discussed above, including the ming and amount of our future income.

If Blackstone Inc. were deemed an “investment company” under the 1940 Act, applicable restricons could make it impraccal for us
to connue our business as contemplated and could have a material adverse eﬀect on our business.

     An enty will generally be deemed to be an “investment company” for purposes of the 1940 Act if: (a) it is or holds itself out as being
engaged primarily, or proposes to engage primarily, in the business of invesng, reinvesng or trading in securies, or (b) absent an
applicable exempon, it owns or proposes to acquire investment securies having a value exceeding 40% of the value of its total assets
(exclusive of U.S. government securies and cash items) on an unconsolidated basis. We hold ourselves out as engaging, and believe that
we are engaged primarily in, the business of providing asset management and capital markets services and not in the business of
invesng, reinvesng or trading in securies. We also believe that the primary source of income from each of our businesses is properly
characterized as income earned in exchange for the provision of services. Accordingly, we do not believe that Blackstone Inc. is an
“orthodox” investment company as described in clause (a) in the ﬁrst sentence of this paragraph. Furthermore, Blackstone Inc. does not
have any material assets other than its general partner interests in the Blackstone Holdings Partnerships and its equity interests in certain
wholly owned subsidiaries (which in turn have no material assets other than intercompany debt). These wholly owned subsidiaries are
the sole general partners of the Blackstone Holdings Partnerships and are vested with all management and control over the Blackstone
Holdings Partnerships. We do not believe these assets are investment securies. Moreover, because we believe that the capital interests
of the general partners of our funds in their respecve funds are neither securies nor investment securies, we believe that less than
40% of Blackstone Inc.’s total assets (exclusive of U.S. government securies and cash items) on an unconsolidated basis are comprised of
assets that could be considered investment securies. Accordingly, we do not believe Blackstone Inc. is an inadvertent investment
company by virtue of the 40% test described in clause (b) in the ﬁrst sentence of this paragraph. In addion, we believe Blackstone Inc. is
not an investment company under Secon 3(b)(1) of the 1940 Act because it is primarily engaged in a non-investment company business.

    The 1940 Act and the rules thereunder contain detailed parameters for the organizaon and operaon of investment companies.
Among other things, the 1940 Act and the rules thereunder limit or prohibit transacons with aﬃliates, impose limitaons on the
issuance of debt and equity securies, generally prohibit the issuance of opons and impose certain governance requirements.
Accordingly, Blackstone Inc. conducts its operaons so that it will not be deemed to be an investment company under the 1940 Act. If
Blackstone Inc. were deemed to be an investment company under the 1940 Act, it would have to comply with rules thereunder, which
could impose limitaons on our capital structure, ability to transact business with aﬃliates and compensate key employees. This could
make it impraccal to connue our business as currently conducted, impair the agreements and arrangements between and among
Blackstone Inc., Blackstone Holdings and our senior managing directors, or any combinaon thereof, and materially adversely aﬀect our
business, ﬁnancial condion and results of operaons.

Item 1C.   Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity Risk Management and Strategy

    Blackstone maintains a comprehensive cybersecurity program, including policies and procedures designed to protect our systems,
operaons and the data entrusted to us by our investors, employees, porolio companies and business partners from ancipated threats
or hazards. Blackstone ulizes a variety of protecve measures as a part of its cybersecurity program. These measures include, where
appropriate, physical and digital access controls, patch management, identy veriﬁcaon and mobile device management so ware, new
hire and annual employee cybersecurity awareness and best pracces training programs, security baselines and tools to report
anomalous acvity, and monitoring of data usage, hardware and so ware.

    We test our cybersecurity defenses regularly through automated and manual vulnerability scanning, to idenfy and remediate crical
vulnerabilies. In addion, we conduct annual “white hat” penetraon tests to validate our security posture. We internally review our
cybersecurity program and conduct a third-party review every two to three years to evaluate its eﬀecveness, in part by considering
industry standards and established frameworks, such as the Naonal Instute of Standards and Technology and Center for Internet
Security, as guidelines. Further, we engage in cybersecurity incident tabletop exercises and scenario planning exercises involving
hypothecal cybersecurity incidents to test our cybersecurity incident response processes. Our Chief Security Oﬃcer (the “CSO”) and
members of senior management, Legal and Compliance, Technology and Innovaons (“BXTI”) and Global Corporate Aﬀairs parcipate in
these exercises. Learnings from these tabletop exercises and any cybersecurity events we experience are reviewed, discussed and
incorporated into our cybersecurity incident response processes, as appropriate.

    In addion to our internal exercises to test aspects of our cybersecurity program, we periodically engage independent third pares to
analyze data on the interacons of users of our informaon technology resources, including employees, and conduct penetraon tests
and scanning exercises to assess the performance of our cybersecurity systems and processes.

    We have a comprehensive Security Incident Response Plan (the “IRP”) designed to inform the proper escalaon of non-roune
suspected or conﬁrmed informaon security or cybersecurity events based on the expected risk an event presents. As appropriate, a
Security Incident Response Team composed of individuals from several internal technical and managerial funcons may be formed to
invesgate and remediate the event and determine the extent of external advisor support required, including from external counsel,
forensic invesgators, and/or law enforcement. The IRP sets out ongoing monitoring or remediaon acons to be taken a er resoluon
of an incident. The IRP is reviewed at least annually by members of BXTI and Legal and Compliance.

    Blackstone maintains a formal cybersecurity risk management process and cybersecurity risk register, designed to idenfy, track and
treat cybersecurity risks at the ﬁrm, and integrates these processes into the ﬁrm’s overall risk management pracces described above.
Our CSO periodically discusses and reviews cybersecurity risks and related migants with our enterprise risk commiee and incorporates
relevant cybersecurity risk updates and metrics in the semi-annual enterprise-wide risk management report.

    Blackstone has a process designed to assess the cybersecurity risks associated with the engagement of third-party vendors. This
assessment is conducted on the basis of, among other factors, the types of services provided and the extent and type of Blackstone data
accessed or processed by a third-party vendor. On the basis of its preliminary risk assessment of a third-party vendor, Blackstone may
conduct further cybersecurity reviews or request remediaon of, or contractual protecons related to, any actual or potenal idenﬁed
cybersecurity risks. In addion, where appropriate, Blackstone seeks to include in its contractual arrangements with certain of its third-
party vendors provisions addressing its requirements and industry best pracces with respect to data and cybersecurity, as well as the
right to assess, monitor, audit and test such vendors’ cybersecurity programs and pracces. Blackstone also ulizes a number of digital
controls, which are reviewed at least annually, to monitor and manage third-party access to its internal systems and data.

Our Business

    Blackstone is the world’s largest alternave asset manager. Our business is organized into four segments: Real Estate, Private Equity,
Credit & Insurance and Mul-Asset Invesng. For more informaon about our business segments, see “Part I. Item 1. Business

     We generate revenue from fees earned pursuant to contractual arrangements with funds, fund investors and fund porolio

and assuming certain investment returns are achieved, we are entled to a disproporonate allocaon of the income otherwise allocable
to the limited partners, commonly referred to as carried interest (“Performance Allocaons”). In certain investment fund structures, we
receive a contractual incenve fee from the fund based on achieving certain investment returns (an “Incenve Fee,” and together with
Performance Allocaons, “Performance Revenues”). The composion of our revenues will vary based on market condions and the
cyclicality of the diﬀerent business units we operate. Net investment gains and investment income generated by Blackstone Funds are
driven by the performance of underlying investments in such funds as well as overall market condions. Fair values are aﬀected by
changes in the fundamentals of our funds’ porolio companies and other investments, the industries in which they operate, the overall
economy and other market condions.

Business Environment

    Blackstone’s businesses are materially aﬀected by condions in the ﬁnancial markets and economic condions in the U.S., Europe,
Asia and, to a lesser extent, elsewhere in the world.

     Most major equity markets appreciated in the fourth quarter of 2025, driven by posive economic data and accommodave central
bank acons. The total return of the S&P 500 Index was 2.7% in the fourth quarter, led by the healthcare and telecommunicaons
sectors, which gained 11.7% and 7.3%, respecvely. The real estate and ulies sectors underperformed, declining 2.9% and 1.4%,
respecvely. Equity market volality decreased, with the CBOE Volality Index (VIX) declining 8.2% at the end of the fourth quarter
compared to the third quarter. In credit markets, the S&P Leveraged Loan Index generated a total return of 1.2% and the ICE Bank of
America High Yield Bond Index returned 1.3%. At the beginning of 2026, however, concerns regarding impact of arﬁcial intelligence-
driven disrupon weighed on equity capital markets. By mid-February 2026, the Dow Jones and S&P 500 Index had experienced declines
for four out of ﬁve weeks, while the Nasdaq recorded its ﬁ h straight negave week.

    Capital markets acvity levels in the U.S. expanded considerably in 2025, with U.S. inial public oﬀering volumes and announced
merger and acquision volumes up approximately 73% and 60%, respecvely, compared to 2024. In parcular, the fourth quarter saw a
two-and-a-half year-over-year increase in merger and acquision and inial public oﬀerings acvity. High-yield spreads ghtened by
21 basis points in 2025, while issuance increased 16.8% year-over-year.

     While the U.S. economy exhibited steady growth through most of 2025, the Bureau of Economic Analysis’ advance esmate of U.S.
real GDP annualized growth was 1.4% in the fourth quarter. This was well below esmates, and the Bureau esmated, among other
factors, that the U.S. government shutdown subtracted about 1.0% from such expected GDP growth. The labor market remained largely
in balance, with an unemployment rate of 4.4% at year end, up moderately from 4.1% at year-end 2024. Inﬂaon decreased over the
course of 2025, with headline CPI of 2.7% in December 2025 compared to 3.0% in January 2025. The Federal Reserve decreased the
federal funds target range three mes in 2025 to 3.50-3.75% by year end and held rates steady in January 2026, based on its view that
inﬂaon has remained above the target rate of 2%.

    Outside of the U.S., most major central banks reduced interest rates in 2025 as inﬂaon around the world connued to show signs of
moderaon. Inﬂaon in the U.K. increased slightly to 3.4% in December 2025 compared to 3.0% in January 2025, but remained well

The European Central Bank lowered its deposit facility by 100 basis points during the year, with inﬂaon in the Eurozone falling to 1.9% in

    An overall resilient economic backdrop, alongside moderang interest rates in several major economies, supported a gradual

disrupons across a number of industries, however, have more recently adversely impacted investor senment and the market

Key Financial Measures and Indicators

    We manage our business using certain ﬁnancial measures and key operang metrics since we believe these metrics measure the
producvity of our investment acvies. We prepare our consolidated ﬁnancial statements in accordance with accounng principles
generally accepted in the United States of America (“GAAP”). See “—Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data — Notes to
Consolidated Financial Statements — Note 2. Summary of Signiﬁcant Accounng Policies” and “—Crical Accounng Policies.” Our key
non-GAAP ﬁnancial measures and operang indicators and metrics are discussed below.

Distributable Earnings

    Distributable Earnings is derived from Blackstone’s segment reported results. Distributable Earnings is used to assess performance
and amounts available for dividends to Blackstone stockholders, including Blackstone personnel and others who are limited partners of
the Blackstone Holdings Partnerships. Distributable Earnings is the sum of Segment Distributable Earnings plus Net Interest and Dividend
Income (Loss) less Taxes and Related Payables. Distributable Earnings excludes unrealized acvity and is derived from and reconciled to,
but not equivalent to, its most directly comparable GAAP measure of Income (Loss) Before Provision (Beneﬁt) for Taxes. See
“—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for our reconciliaon of Distributable Earnings.

                                                                                                                                      82
    Net Interest and Dividend Income (Loss) is presented on a segment basis and is equal to Interest and Dividend Revenue less Interest
Expense, adjusted for the impact of consolidaon of Blackstone Funds, and interest expense associated with the Tax Receivable
Agreement.

     Taxes and Related Payables represent the total GAAP tax provision adjusted to include only the current tax provision (beneﬁt)
calculated on Income (Loss) Before Provision (Beneﬁt) for Taxes and including the payable under the Tax Receivable Agreement. Further,
the current tax provision ulized when calculang Taxes and Related Payables and Distributable Earnings reﬂects the beneﬁt of
deducons available to the company on certain expense items that are excluded from the underlying calculaon of Segment Distributable
Earnings and Total Segment Distributable Earnings, such as equity-based compensaon charges and certain Transacon-Related and
Non-Recurring Items where there is a current tax provision or beneﬁt. The economic assumpons and methodologies that impact the
implied income tax provision are the same as those methodologies and assumpons used in calculang the current income tax provision
for Blackstone’s Consolidated Statements of Operaons under GAAP, excluding the impact of divestures and accrued tax conngency-
related liabilies or refunds which are reﬂected when paid or received. The Payable under the Tax Receivable Agreement reﬂects the
expected amount of tax savings generated in the period that pares to the Tax Receivable Agreement are entled to receive in future
periods. Management believes that including the amount payable under the Tax Receivable Agreement and ulizing the current income
tax provision adjusted as described above when calculang Distributable Earnings is meaningful as it increases comparability between
periods and more accurately reﬂects earnings that are available for distribuon to stockholders.

Segment Distributable Earnings

    Segment Distributable Earnings is Blackstone’s segment proﬁtability measure used to make operang decisions and assess
performance across Blackstone’s four segments. Blackstone believes it is useful to stockholders to review the measure that management
uses in assessing segment performance. Segment Distributable Earnings represents the net realized earnings of Blackstone’s segments
and is the sum of Fee Related Earnings and Net Realizaons for each segment. Blackstone’s segments are presented on a basis that
deconsolidates Blackstone Funds, eliminates non-controlling ownership interests in Blackstone’s consolidated operang partnerships,
removes the amorzaon of intangible assets and removes Transacon-Related and Non-Recurring Items. Transacon-Related and
Non-Recurring Items arise from corporate acons including acquisions, divestures, Blackstone’s inial public oﬀering and non-recurring
gains, losses, or other charges, if any. They consist primarily of equity-based compensaon charges, gains and losses on conngent
consideraon arrangements, changes in the balance of the Tax Receivable Agreement resulng from a change in tax law or similar event,
transacon costs, gains or losses associated with these corporate acons and non-recurring gains, losses or other charges that aﬀect
period-to-period comparability and are not reﬂecve of Blackstone’s operaonal performance. Segment Distributable Earnings excludes
unrealized acvity and is derived from and reconciled to, but not equivalent to, its most directly comparable GAAP measure of Income
(Loss) Before Provision (Beneﬁt) for Taxes. See “—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for our reconciliaon of Segment Distributable
Earnings.

    Net Realizaons is presented on a segment basis and is the sum of Realized Principal Investment Income and Realized Performance
Revenues (which refers to Realized Performance Revenues excluding Fee Related Performance Revenues), less Realized Performance
Compensaon (which refers to Realized Performance Compensaon excluding Fee Related Performance Compensaon and Equity-Based
Performance Compensaon).

    Realized Performance Compensaon reﬂects, pursuant to an ongoing compensaon program, an increase in the aggregate Realized
Performance Compensaon paid to certain of our professionals above the amounts allocable to them based upon the percentage
parcipaon in the relevant performance plans previously awarded to them. For the year ended December 31, 2025, Realized
Performance Compensaon increased by an aggregate of $76.6 million and Fee Related Compensaon decreased by a corresponding
amount. For the year ended December 31, 2024, Realized Performance Compensaon increased by an aggregate of $83.1 million and Fee

                                                                                                                                      83
Related Compensaon decreased by a corresponding amount. These changes to Realized Performance Compensaon and Fee Related
Compensaon reduced Net Realizaons, increased Fee Related Earnings and had a neutral impact to Income Before Provision (Beneﬁt)
for Taxes and Distributable Earnings for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024.

Fee Related Earnings

     Fee Related Earnings is a performance measure used to assess Blackstone’s ability to generate proﬁts from revenues that are
measured and received on a recurring basis and not subject to future realizaon events. Blackstone believes Fee Related Earnings is
useful to stockholders as it provides insight into the proﬁtability of the poron of Blackstone’s business that is not dependent on
realizaon acvity. Fee Related Earnings equals management and advisory fees (net of management fee reducons and oﬀsets) plus Fee
Related Performance Revenues, less (a) Fee Related Compensaon on a segment basis and (b) Other Operang Expenses. Fee Related
Earnings is derived from and reconciled to, but not equivalent to, its most directly comparable GAAP measure of Income (Loss) Before
Provision (Beneﬁt) for Taxes. See “—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for our reconciliaon of Fee Related Earnings.

    Fee Related Compensaon is presented on a segment basis and refers to the compensaon expense, excluding Equity-Based
Compensaon, directly related to (a) Management and Advisory Fees, Net and (b) Fee Related Performance Revenues, referred to as Fee
Related Performance Compensaon.

    Fee Related Performance Revenues refers to the realized poron of Performance Revenues from Perpetual Capital that are
(a) measured and received on a recurring basis and (b) not dependent on realizaon events from the underlying investments.

     Other Operang Expenses is presented on a segment basis and is equal to General, Administrave and Other Expenses, adjusted to
(a) remove transacon-related and non-recurring items that arise from corporate acons including acquisions, divestures, Blackstone’s
inial public oﬀering and non-recurring gains, losses or other charges, if any, (b) remove certain expenses reimbursed by the Blackstone
Funds which are need against Management and Advisory Fees, Net in Blackstone’s segment presentaon and (c) give eﬀect to an
administrave fee collected on a quarterly basis from certain holders of Blackstone Holdings Partnership Units. The administrave fee is
accounted for as a capital contribuon under GAAP, but is reﬂected as a reducon of Other Operang Expenses in Blackstone’s segment
presentaon.

Adjusted Earnings Before Interest, Taxes and Depreciaon and Amorzaon

     Adjusted Earnings Before Interest, Taxes and Depreciaon and Amorzaon (“Adjusted EBITDA”), is a supplemental measure used to
assess performance derived from Blackstone’s segment results and may be used to assess its ability to service its borrowings. Adjusted
EBITDA represents Distributable Earnings plus the addion of (a) Interest Expense on a segment basis, (b) Taxes and Related Payables and
(c) Depreciaon and Amorzaon. Adjusted EBITDA is derived from and reconciled to, but not equivalent to, its most directly comparable
GAAP measure of Income (Loss) Before Provision (Beneﬁt) for Taxes. See “—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for our reconciliaon of
Adjusted EBITDA.

Net Accrued Performance Revenues

    Net Accrued Performance Revenues is a non-GAAP ﬁnancial measure Blackstone believes is useful to stockholders as an indicator of
potenal future realized performance revenues based on the current investment porolio of the funds and vehicles we manage. Net
Accrued Performance Revenues represents the accrued performance revenues receivable by Blackstone, net of the related accrued
performance compensaon payable by Blackstone, excluding performance revenues that have been realized but not yet distributed as of
the reporng date and clawback amounts, if any. Net Accrued Performance Revenues is derived from and reconciled to, but not

                                                                                                                                      84
equivalent to, its most directly comparable GAAP measure of Investments. See “—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for our reconciliaon
of Net Accrued Performance Revenues and Note 2. “Summary of Signiﬁcant Accounng Policies — Equity Method Investments” in the
“Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements” in “—Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data” for addional informaon on
the calculaon of Investments — Accrued Performance Allocaons.

Operang Metrics

    The alternave asset management business is primarily based on managing third-party capital and does not require substanal
capital investment to support rapid growth. Since our incepon, we have developed and used various key operang metrics to assess and
monitor the operang performance of our various alternave asset management businesses in order to monitor the eﬀecveness of our
value-creang strategies.

Total and Fee-Earning Assets Under Management

    “Total Assets Under Management” refers to the invested and available capital in Blackstone-managed or advised vehicles (including,
without limitaon, investment funds and SMAs). The Total Assets Under Management aributable to an individual vehicle is dependent
on the structure and investment strategy of such vehicle and accordingly, will vary from vehicle to vehicle. Total Assets Under
Management generally equals the sum of the following across Blackstone-managed or advised vehicles, as applicable:

    (a) a vehicle’s invested capital at fair value which, as applicable, is measured as (1) total investments measured at fair value, or
          gross asset values, each of which may include the fair value of investments purchased with leverage under certain credit
          facilies, (2) net asset value, or (3) amount of debt and equity outstanding or aggregate par amount of assets, including
          principal cash for CLOs, and
    (b) a vehicle’s available capital, if any, which represents (1) uncalled commitments made by investors and (2) available borrowing
          capacity under certain credit facilies.

    Uncalled commitments represent the capital we are entled to call from investors pursuant to the terms of their respecve capital
commitments, including capital commitments to funds that have yet to commence their investment periods. Drawdown funds, perpetual
capital vehicles, co-investment vehicles, and SMAs can each be structured with a commitment from an investor that is called over me as
opposed to fully funded upon subscripon.

    Assets may be raised in one vehicle or business unit and subsequently invested in or managed or advised by another vehicle or
business unit. Total Assets Under Management are reported in the segment where the assets are managed.

    Our measurement of Total Assets Under Management includes commitments to, and the fair value of, invested capital in our funds
from Blackstone and our personnel. Our calculaon of Total Assets Under Management may diﬀer from the calculaons of other asset
managers, and as a result this measure may not be comparable to similar measures presented by other asset managers. Our deﬁnion of
Total Assets Under Management diﬀers from the manner in which aﬃliated investment advisors report regulatory assets under
management and may diﬀer from the deﬁnion set forth in the agreements governing the vehicles we manage or advise.

     “Fee-Earning Assets Under Management” refers to the poron of Total Assets Under Management on which we are entled to earn
management fees and/or performance revenues. The Fee-Earning Assets Under Management aributable to an individual vehicle is
driven by the basis on which fees are earned and accordingly, will vary from vehicle to vehicle. Fee-Earning Assets Under Management
generally equals the sum of the following across Blackstone-managed or advised vehicles, as applicable: (a) net asset value,
(b) commied capital and remaining invested capital during the investment period and post-investment period, respecvely, (c) invested
capital (including leverage to the extent management fee-eligible), (d) gross asset value, (e) fair value of investments, or (f) the aggregate
par amount of collateral assets, including principal cash, of CLOs.

                                                                                                                                            85
    Assets may be raised in one vehicle or business unit and subsequently invested in or managed or advised by another vehicle or
business unit. Fee-Earning Assets Under Management are reported in the segment where the Total Assets Under Management are
reported to the extent fee-paying to Blackstone.

    While Fee-Earning Assets Under Management generally reﬂects Total Assets Under Management on which we are entled to earn
management fees, Fee-Earning Assets Under Management may also include Total Assets Under Management on which we are entled to
earn only performance revenues. Our calculaon of Fee-Earning Assets Under Management may diﬀer from the calculaons of other
asset managers, and as a result this measure may not be comparable to similar measures presented by other asset managers. Our
deﬁnion of Fee-Earning Assets Under Management may diﬀer from the deﬁnion set forth in the agreements governing the vehicles
that we manage or advise.

    Commitment-based drawdown structured funds generally do not permit investors to redeem their interests at their elecon. Certain
of our open-ended vehicles generally aﬀord an investor the right to withdraw or redeem their interests on a periodic basis (for example,
annually, quarterly or monthly), typically with 2 to 95 days’ noce, depending on the fund and the liquidity proﬁle of the underlying
assets. In our perpetual capital vehicles where redempon rights exist, redempon requests are required to be fulﬁlled only (a) in
Blackstone’s or the vehicles’ board’s discreon, as applicable, (b) to the extent there is suﬃcient new capital, or (c) where such required
redempons are limited in quantum, such as interval funds or in certain insurance-dedicated vehicles. Investment advisory agreements
related to certain SMAs in our Credit & Insurance and Mul-Asset Invesng segments, excluding SMAs in our insurance plaorm, may
generally be terminated by an investor on 15 to 95 days’ noce. SMAs in our insurance plaorm can generally only be terminated for
long-term underperformance, cause and certain other limited circumstances, in each case subject to Blackstone’s right to cure.

Perpetual Capital

    “Perpetual Capital” refers to the component of assets under management with an indeﬁnite term, that is not in liquidaon, and for
which there is no requirement to return capital to investors through redempon requests in the ordinary course of business, except
where funded by new capital inﬂows or where required redempons are limited in quantum. Perpetual Capital includes co-investment
capital with an investor right to convert into Perpetual Capital.

    In our Perpetual Capital vehicles where redempon rights exist, redempon requests are required to be fulﬁlled only (a) in
Blackstone’s or the vehicles’ board’s discreon, as applicable, (b) to the extent there is suﬃcient new capital, or (c) where such required
redempons are limited in quantum, such as interval funds or in certain insurance-dedicated vehicles. Perpetual Capital includes
co-investment capital with an investor right to convert into Perpetual Capital. We believe this measure is useful to stockholders as it
represents capital we manage that has a longer duraon and the ability to generate recurring revenues in a diﬀerent manner than
tradional fund structures.

Dry Powder

    Dry Powder represents the amount of capital available for investment or reinvestment, including general partner and employee
capital, and is an indicator of the capital we have available for future investments. We believe this measure is useful to stockholders as it
provides insight into the extent to which capital is available for Blackstone to deploy capital into investment opportunies as they arise.

                                                                                                                                            86
Invested Performance Eligible Assets Under Management

     Invested Performance Eligible Assets Under Management represents invested capital at fair value on which performance revenues
could be earned if certain hurdles are met. We believe Invested Performance Eligible Assets Under Management is useful to stockholders
as it provides insight into the capital deployed that has the potenal to generate performance revenues.

Year Ended December 31, 2025 Compared to Year Ended December 31, 2024

Revenues

    Revenues were $14.5 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $1.2 billion, compared to $13.2 billion for the year
ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Revenues was primarily aributable to increases of $886.7 million in Management and
Advisory Fees, Net and $709.2 million in Investment Income (Loss).

    Management and Advisory Fees, Net were $8.1 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $886.7 million,
compared to $7.2 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Management and Advisory Fees, Net was primarily
aributable to increases in our Private Equity and Credit & Insurance segments of $573.3 million and $347.8 million, respecvely. The
increase in our Private Equity segment was primarily aributable to an increase in Base Management Fees due to fee holiday expiraons
of BCP IX and BETP IV, an increase in Fee-Earning Assets Under Management in BXPE and BIP, and increased deal acvity in BXCM. The
increase in our Credit & Insurance segment was primarily aributable to an increase in Base Management Fees due to increased
Fee-Earning Assets Under Management in private credit strategies.

    Investment Income (Loss) was $5.3 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $709.2 million, compared to
$4.5 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Investment Income (Loss) was primarily aributable to an increase of
$569.9 million in Realized Investment Income. The increase in Realized Investment Income was primarily aributable to higher realized
gains during the year ended December 31, 2025 compared to the year ended December 31, 2024. The principal driver of this increase
was an increase of $406.7 million in our Credit & Insurance segment which was primarily aributable to the sale of Bistro, a porolio
visualizaon so ware plaorm developed by Blackstone, and the monezaon of Blackstone’s stake in Resoluon Life.

Expenses

    Expenses were $7.7 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $883.3 million, compared to $6.8 billion for the
year ended December 31, 2024. The increase was primarily aributable to an increase of $626.5 million in Total Compensaon and
Beneﬁts, of which $623.0 million was an increase in Compensaon. The increase in Compensaon was primarily aributable to the
increase in Management and Advisory Fees, Net, on which a poron of Compensaon is based.

Other Income (Loss)

    Other Income was $424.0 million for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $375.2 million, compared to $48.8 million for
the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Other Income was primarily aributable to an increase of $327.3 million in Net Gains
from Fund Investment Acvies.

    The increase in Net Gains from Fund Investment Acvies was primarily aributable to increases of $172.8 million in our Real Estate
segment and $123.9 million in our Private Equity segment. The increase in our Real Estate segment was primarily aributable to net
unrealized appreciaon of investments in our consolidated funds in the year ended December 31, 2025 compared to net unrealized
depreciaon of investments in the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in our Private Equity segment was primarily aributable
to higher net unrealized appreciaon of investments in our consolidated funds in the year ended December 31, 2025 compared to the
year ended December 31, 2024.

Provision for Taxes

    Blackstone’s Provision for Taxes for the year ended December 31, 2025 was $1.1 billion, an increase of $103.4 million, compared to
$1.0 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024. This resulted in an eﬀecve tax rate of 15.7% and 15.8%, based on our Income Before
Provision for Taxes of $7.2 billion and $6.5 billion for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, respecvely.

    Total Assets Under Management and Fee-Earning Assets Under Management may have diﬀerences in the measurement and ming of
certain acvies that aﬀect each of inﬂows, oulows, realizaons and market acvity. These diﬀerences include, but are not limited to:

    •      For commitment-based drawdown funds, Total Assets Under Management inﬂows are generally reported at each fund closing
           whereas Fee-Earning Assets Under Management inﬂows are generally reported when a fund’s investment period commences.
           Fund closings and the investment period commencement generally occur in diﬀerent periods and as such, Fee-Earning Assets
           Under Management inﬂows in such funds may exceed Total Assets Under Management inﬂows in the period when the
           investment period commences. This is most prevalent in our Real Estate and Private Equity segments.
    •      For commitment-based drawdown funds, Total Assets Under Management realizaons generally represents the total proceeds
           whereas Fee-Earning Assets Under Management generally represents only the invested capital. As such, Total Assets Under
           Management realizaons typically exceeds Fee-Earning Assets Under Management realizaons. This is most prevalent in our
           Real Estate and Private Equity segments.
    •      For commitment-based drawdown funds, Total Assets Under Management is reported based on invested capital at fair value
           and available capital whereas Fee-Earning Assets Under Management is reported based on commied or remaining invested
           capital. As such, Total Assets Under Management market acvity generally exceeds Fee-Earning Assets Under Management
           market acvity. This is most prevalent in our Real Estate and Private Equity segments.

                                                                                                                                                94
    •     For certain credit funds, Total Assets Under Management are based on gross asset value while Fee-Earning Assets Under
          Management are based on net asset value. As such, Total Assets Under Management inﬂows, oulows, realizaons and
          market acvity for the period generally exceed the Fee-Earning Assets Under Management inﬂows, oulows, realizaons and
          market acvity for the period.

Year Ended December 31, 2025 Compared to Year Ended December 31, 2024

    Segment Distributable Earnings were $2.4 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $222.5 million, compared to
$2.1 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Segment Distributable Earnings was aributable to an increase of
$187.9 million in Fee Related Earnings and an increase of $34.6 million in Net Realizaons.

    Given the gradual pace of the real estate recovery over the course of 2025, the funds in our Real Estate segment saw limited
appreciaon in aggregate, notwithstanding strong performance in BREIT. Connued and signiﬁcant strength in digital infrastructure
investments supported performance in the year, which was parally oﬀset by more challenging fundamentals in life sciences oﬃce,
student housing and select logiscs holdings. We believe there are a number of posive signs that should support values in our Real
Estate porolio, including favorable capital markets and declining new supply. Connued improvement in the cost and availability of debt
also contributes to an environment that is more conducive to increased transacon volume.

Year Ended December 31, 2025 Compared to Year Ended December 31, 2024

    Segment Distributable Earnings were $2.9 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $268.0 million, compared to

    Our Private Equity segment generated strong performance across all strategies in 2025, with parcular strength in Infrastructure. In
Corporate Private Equity, our operang companies exhibited solid revenue growth and resilient margins. A more favorable capital markets
environment supported an acceleraon in transacon acvity, parcularly inial public oﬀerings, in our Private Equity segment funds in
the second half of 2025. A connuaon of a favorable capital markets environment should contribute to a further increase in transacon
acvity, including realizaons, in our Private Equity segment. Despite an overall strong capital markets environment, the potenal for
arﬁcial intelligence-driven disrupon has recently weighed on equity capital markets and equity values of companies in certain sectors,
such as so ware. We believe the ulmate impact of such disrupon will vary signiﬁcantly across companies based on mulple factors,
with a number of companies well-posioned to be protected or beneﬁt from such disrupon. We believe such factors, which include
large company size, depth of resources and high customer switching costs, are generally evident across our porolio.

Funds With Closed Investment Periods as of December 31, 2025

    Corporate Private Equity has nine funds with closed investment periods: BCP V, BCP VI, BCP VII, BCP VIII, BEP I, BEP II, BEP III, BCEP I
and BCP Asia I. BCP V is comprised of two fund classes, the BCP V “main fund” and BCP V-AC fund. Within these fund classes, the general
partner is subject to equalizaon such that (a) the general partner accrues carried interest when the respecve carried interest for either
fund class is posive and (b) the general partner realizes carried interest so long as clawback obligaons, if any, for either of the
respecve fund classes are fully sasﬁed. BCP V, BCP VI, BCP VII, BCP VIII, BEP I, BEP II, BEP III, BCEP I and BCP Asia I were above their
respecve carried interest thresholds. Funds are considered above their carried interest thresholds based on the aggregate fund posion,
although individual limited partners may be below their respecve carried interest thresholds in certain funds.

     Taccal Opportunies has various funds with closed investment periods, which are each above their carried interest thresholds based
on aggregate fund posion. Blackstone Growth has one fund with a closed investment period, BXG I, which is not above its carried
interest threshold. Secondaries has various funds with closed investment periods, including but not limited to: Strategic Partners
Infrastructure III, Strategic Partners VIII, Strategic Partners Real Estate VII and BSCH I which are above their respecve carried interest
thresholds based on aggregate fund posion. Blackstone Life Sciences has funds with a closed investment period: Clarus IV, BXLS V and
BXLS Yield, which are each above their carried interest thresholds.

Year Ended December 31, 2025 Compared to Year Ended December 31, 2024

    Segment Distributable Earnings were $2.0 billion for the year ended December 31, 2025, an increase of $533.4 million, compared to
$1.4 billion for the year ended December 31, 2024. The increase in Segment Distributable Earnings was aributable to increases of
$195.4 million in Fee Related Earnings and $338.0 million in Net Realizaons.

     Our Credit & Insurance segment demonstrated strong performance in 2025. While lower interest rates will likely reduce returns in
our ﬂoang rate strategies, we believe we will connue to generate excess returns relave to liquid markets in our private credit
strategies. We also connue to see long-term structural shi s toward private credit in the credit market. This has contributed to robust
momentum in our non-investment grade and investment grade private credit strategies. Opportunies for corporate and bank
partnerships should also support momentum in investment grade private credit strategies. While we would expect defaults to rise from a
historically low level as the credit cycle progresses, our Credit & Insurance segment funds’ holdings are predominantly in senior secured
credit with signiﬁcant equity subordinaon from instuonal borrowers. We believe this should posion our Credit & Insurance segment
well. A favorable capital markets environment has supported, and should connue to support, overall transacon acvity in our Credit &
Insurance segment. Nevertheless, despite an overall strong capital markets environment, the potenal for arﬁcial intelligence-driven
disrupon has recently weighed on the equity capital markets and on equity values of companies in certain sectors, such as so ware. We
believe the ulmate impact of such disrupon will vary signiﬁcantly across companies based on mulple factors, and that companies that
are larger, have depth of resources and whose customers face high switching costs, are well-posioned to be protected or beneﬁt from
such disrupon. Notwithstanding the potenal for arﬁcial-intelligence disrupon, we believe our overall porolio is relavely well-
protected given the extent of our equity cushion and the prevalence of such factors at companies in our porolio.

   In our perpetual capital strategies, BCRED maintained healthy demand with over $14 billion raised in 2025. While heightened market
aenon around private credit has and could connue to adversely aﬀect net ﬂows, we believe that strong investment performance
should drive ﬂows over the long-term.

Liquidity and Capital Resources

General

    Blackstone’s business model derives revenue primarily from third-party Assets Under Management. Blackstone is not a capital or
balance sheet intensive business and targets operang expense levels such that total management and advisory fees exceed total
operang expenses each period. As a result, we require limited capital resources to support the working capital or operang needs of our
businesses. We draw primarily on the long-term commied or invested capital of investors in our investment vehicles to fund the
investment requirements of the Blackstone Funds and use our own realizaons and cash ﬂows to invest in growth iniaves, make
commitments to our own funds, where our minimum general partner commitments are generally less than 5% of the limited partner
commitments of a fund, and pay dividends to stockholders and distribuons to holders of Holdings Units.

    Fluctuaons in our statement of ﬁnancial condion result primarily from acvies of the Blackstone Funds that are consolidated as
well as business transacons, such as the issuance of senior notes. The majority economic ownership interests of such consolidated
Blackstone Funds are reﬂected as Redeemable Non-Controlling Interests in Consolidated Enes, and Non-Controlling Interests in
Consolidated Enes in the consolidated ﬁnancial statements. The consolidaon of these Blackstone Funds has no net eﬀect on
Blackstone’s Net Income or Equity. Addionally, ﬂuctuaons in our statement of ﬁnancial condion also include appreciaon or
depreciaon in Blackstone investments in the non-consolidated Blackstone Funds, addional investments and redempons of such
interests in the non-consolidated Blackstone Funds and the collecon of receivables related to management and advisory fees.

    Total Assets were $47.7 billion as of December 31, 2025, an increase of $4.2 billion from December 31, 2024. The increase in Total
Assets was primarily aributable to increases of $2.8 billion in total assets aributable to consolidated operang partnerships and
$1.6 billion in total assets aributable to consolidated Blackstone funds.
